content.summary_of_the_paper:
Inspired by neuronal dynamics, the authors propose a neural network model based on interacting particles (so-called sub-modules). They derive the update rules from the Euler-Lagrange equations under energy and momentum conservation constraints.
The model classifies images slightly more accurately than a vanilla 2-layer NN on the MNIST dataset and significantly better than several standard architectures on ImageNet when these were disturbed in their parameters to account for the loss of model information during physical implementation. Also, their model needs fewer (yet more complex) units and lower computational complexity when excluding the path integral computation, which would be computed by the physical system if instantiated.
They also show that a higher disturbance of the model (leading to lower performance) correlates with structural entropy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is nicely formatted, and the figures are clean, sufficiently high resolution and aesthetically pleasing.
The setting and motivation are interesting. In biology, neuronal dynamics (dynamics within the nerve cell/neuron) are relevant for computation while in artificial neural networks the “neuron” is very simplistic.

The method description could be significantly clearer
Figure and table captions need to be more descriptivesoat one can quickly gain an overview without needing to search the main text.
- Figure 1 a) Explanation for what the colors mean missing (only hinted at in joint caption, but explicit only in the main text), related to that: Why are red and blue in a different order in spiking NNs? Consider a larger font size for better readability. 
- Figure 1 b) What does the color scale mean? What are the moving circles: are they depicting the modules at different time steps? It becomes clearer from the main text but not from the figure alone.
- Figure 1 joint caption only describes b), so maybe more appropriate as a caption there. What is the main difference between weights-based and dynamics-based/inspired NNs? How does the figure highlight that?
- Figure 2: more prominent labels. Maybe use words instead of mathematical symbols for faster comprehension by the reader. In general, it isn't easy to gain a feeling for what the method does, given just this figure. Try to make the difference to standard neural networks clearer.
- Figure 4 a) What are the four different colors? Labels seem wrong, as accuracy cannot be both an axis and a label.
- Table 2: Caption should make metrics clear. Clearly describe in the caption what are HUs (hidden units?)/ HSMs, TUs, MACs, and REMs so that one can look at the table in isolation (not only in the main text). Also would be instructive to include the number of parameters, as the proposed unit and its dynamic state are more complex than the typical neuron, several trainable parameters may be a more relevant comparison than the number of units. 

The motivation for the paper is unclear to me. How is the fixed structure of neural networks related to the problems of requirements of parameters, gradient vanishing/explosion or “duplicate computations”? Please cite a source for “duplicate computations” what is meant by that?
Is structural learning needed to approximate nonlinear functions of arbitrary complexity (Cybenko’s approximation theorem for neural networks)? (intro, second paragraph)
The last sentence is unclear to me, which boundaries? Isn’t reservoir computing for example only learning numerically? How do boundaries between structural and numerical learning hinder an optimal approximation?
What is meant by mathematically trivial? How does relate to the neurological fact afterwards? (third paragraph). In which regard exactly is the implementation more efficient?

From the related work section, it is unclear how exactly this method improves upon previous approaches. What are the central contributions that other related approaches have not yet explored? 

The experiments are comparing not to related work on dynamics-based NNs, but to standard neural networks. 
The comparison on MNIST shows a small performance increase but does not make clear how consistent this improvement is. When repeating training several times how high is the variance of the accuracy? Maybe include standard deviation over several runs so that it is easier to read off the significance of the improvement. In addition, the practical computational demands, both in model complexity and in necessary computing would be useful information. I assume the eight GPUs were used for the proposed DyN model and not for the 2-layer NN? How much memory is needed for each setting? Also, why is halving the resolution of MNIST necessary for computational reasons? And most importantly, how many trainable parameters (not units) does each model have? Without a practical estimate of the compute and the number of trainable parameters, the reported results on computational complexity can be misleading.
For the experiments on ImageNet, the reported increase in performance is large but only compared to models with altered parameters, supposedly to adjust for the low resolution of physical implementation. For clarity, it would be good to include the performance without such adjustment (for Inception e.g.  79.8% top-1 accuracy from the original paper). Also, the derivation/motivation of this adjustment could be elaborated on: Why exactly is it more realistic? Why would one need to use a noisy physical system for computation? Maybe the motivation for this method could become stronger if this were elaborated on in the introduction.

The writing is overall decent. There are however a lot of errors that could be avoided in by using a grammar checker (e.g. Grammarly, free version). E.g.:
- Introduction first paragraph: duplicated → duplicate, 
- the second paragraph: requires large amount → require a large amount, compared with → compared to, or has not developed → or have not developed 
At times, it seems wordy: e.g. “As another direction of research endeavors” (intro, second paragraph) and overly complicated: “The boundaries between structural and numerical learning hinder the way to find an optimal neural mechanism to approximate the idealized nonlinear functions of arbitrary complexity for a given task.“

content.title: Point-to-Point Response to Reviewer eQSZ (Part I)
content.comment:
Thanks for the constructive comments and suggestions! The responses to the questions are listed below.
 

Q1: Is structural learning needed to approximate nonlinear functions of arbitrary complexity (Cybenko’s approximation theorem for neural networks)? (intro, second paragraph) 

A1: It cannot be directly derived from UAT that the nonlinear functions need structure learning to approximate. However, in reality, the structure of ANN indeed determines how well the nonlinear functions are approximated, which is evidenced by recent advance of deep learning models from AlexNet, to GoogleNet, and to ResNet and then to Transformers. The importance of structure of ANNs is also validated in the related study of dynamic neural networks[a], weight agnostic neural networks[b] and others. Therefore, the structure learning should be emphasized to develop a better learning paradigm.


Q2: The last sentence is unclear to me, which boundaries? How do boundaries between structural and numerical learning hinder an optimal approximation? 

A2: Normally, we mean that the structural and the numerical learning can hardly be learned simultaneously, or if so, the structural learning is implemented via numerical learning. However, the latter case still requires design of additional structural search and evaluation that are computationally non-trivial. Therefore, we aim to find a better way for conduction structural and numerical learning in our study. Accordingly, we have revised the paper for more clarity.


Q3: Isn’t reservoir computing for example only learning numerically?

A3: Sorry for the misinterpretation on reservior computing. We have corrected it in the revision.


Q4: Unclear motivation && Relation between fixed structure and the problems of parameters, gradient vanishing/explosion or “duplicate computations”?

A4:  We aim to analyze the disadvantage of traditional ANN from the neuromorphic aspects and the UAT, theoretic foundation of ANN. Specifically, as the Cybenko’s universal approximation theorem states, any nonlinear function can be approximated by a neuron. Accordingly, the approximation is undertaken by updating weights w.r.t. their gradients. Only when we construct an ANN with a predefined network structure, the gradients for network parameter update can be calculated and the back propagation can be functioning. However, it is well known that traditional ANN suffers from the gradient vanish/explosion, due to the usage of sigmoid function to endow ANN with nonlinearity to approximate any function. This phenomenon constantly occurs on ANN with more layers, and correspondingly, the number of weight parameters will grow along with the increase of number of layers.  For duplicate computations, we are sorry for the misexpression, which exactly indicates “redundant computations”.
In this paper, we try to address the above issue of traditional ANNs. To this end, we first interpret the ANN as a dynamic system, and derive an equivalent dynamic form of the UAT, which states that any nonlinear function between the S_in and S_out of the submodels in our dynamics-based system can be calculated according to the path integral among neuronal states. What is more important, we theoretically found that the neural weight is equivalent to the covariant of neuronal states while retaining their approximation capacity. Compared to the traditional UATs, we further prove that the dynamic form of UAT has an upper-bounded training computation cost, as discussed in the third paragraph in introduction and Section F in the appendix. More detail can be found in the revised paper.


Q5: Please cite a reference for “duplicate computation” for its meaning.

A5: Over a quite long period, the deep learning community follows the rule that the ANN should be developed to be deeper and deeper, and even over-parametrized. Nevertheless, another side effect also takes place, i.e., the redundant computation, which can be found even in the most elegant models. For example, it has been shown in ResNet [c] that some of the layers are with zero residuals, i.e., they learn nothing. In Capsule network[d], a time-consuming routing mechanism is need to find the optimal connection among capsules, while those capsules off the routes are supposed to be useless. In Spike NN[e], a gating function leads to the fact that only a part of the whole network is taking actions for a specific sample, while the whole network still needs to be maintained. The redundant computation issue has also been studied by recent endeavors. For example, an early exit mechanism is proved to be useful for reducing the computational cost in the inference stage. We are sorry here because of using the term “duplicate computation”, which exactly means “redundant computation”. We have corrected it in the revision.

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
Dear authors, 
thank you for the clarification on several points. From your updated manuscript it is clear that you put a lot of effort into the rebuttal and in the paper in general. 

I still see several errors in the manuscript that should be improved before publication. E.g. Dyn in conclusion but DyN everywhere else, missing articles (third paragraph, from neuromorphic dynamics aspect → from the neuromorphic dynamics aspect), wrong plurals (fifth paragraph, last sentence, different levels of noise), missing spaces (second paragraph, citation after Spiking Neural Networks) and so on. Please use a grammar checker next time!

Empirically,  the motivation for the calculation of parameters is not totally clear to me - that may be my fault though. I am aware that this is a theoretical model and ideally it would be implemented in neuromorphic hardware for optimal efficiency. However, if you need 8 GPUs to run your model to compare it to a small MLP on MNIST (which runs on a conventional CPU just fine), claiming better parameter efficiency and computational complexity is not convincing. 
In general, I think a more suitable comparison would be one of the competitive neuromorphic or bio-plausible methods that you cite in related works and not a generic MLP. The motivation for not using conventional artificial neural networks comes from the desire to be more bio-plausible and enable neuromorphic implementation and not the quantitative improvement on MNIST (on which the performance is saturated anyways).

I can see that you put in a lot of work here and acknowledge that the manuscript has improved, but unfortunately remain unconvinced by the method with its current presentation and empirical results.

content.title: Response to Reviewer eQSZ
content.comment:
Dear reviewer eQSZ,

We highly appreciate your prompt response. We will correct the grammar problems and double-check the manuscript.

For the usage of GPUs, we would like to clarify that we used a Laptop computer with a 2.4 GHz CPU (not GPU) to train a DyN model on MNIST. Training a LeNet5-DyN on this CPU requires less than one hour. The GPUs were only used for training the much bigger models on ImageNet. We usually used only 1 GPU for training our models, like the DyN versions of ResNet-152 or SwinT-S-224. Sorry for not specifying the details in the manuscript. We will clarify this in the revision. 

In fact, the computation complexity of DyN, despite not reaching the best efficiency on the current type of hardware, should never be considered as its drawback compared to existing models. The revised paper has reported the computational complexity (in #FLOPs). Please recheck Tables 1 and 2, where we see clearly that the computational cost has been significantly reduced compared to traditional ANNs.

For the usage of MNIST, we would like to emphasize our purpose again, i.e., using MNIST as a “toy data” to show the learning ability of DyN from scratch and empirically demonstrate how it achieves entropy reduction as derived theoretically. We regret that you neglect all the other experimental phenomenon and only focus on accuracy. We respectively disagree that our model should be rejected for not achieving the best performance on MNIST, while the performance is even more impressive on ImageNet.

For the selection of compared approaches, we agree that it would be better to compare approaches with the neuromorphic implementation described in the introduction part. We will try our best to incorporate the results in the revision. 

However, despite being bio-inspired, all the mentioned neuromorphic implementations achieve inferior results on ImageNet compared to ANN, or they cannot be trained on this dataset. Examples can be found as follows:

      -The differential Spike neural network using ResNet-34 architecture achieves 68.19% top-1 on ImageNet [a], while our DyN model using ResNet-34 architecture achieves 74.56% top-1 on ImageNet, according to our immediate evaluation. It is prohibitive for SNN to use other architectures with more layers and parameters. 

      -The Capsule network performs well on MNIST (99.8x%) but takes a long time to train. It can hardly achieve good results on CIFAR10, not to mention the larger ImageNet dataset.

In comparison, our DyN further improves the strong ViT and Swin-Transformer on ImageNet with much less computation cost, and this fact should be considered when judging the contribution of our work! We are even too modest to claim in the paper that our model can push the neuromorphic models toward a better application perspective, due to its theoretic advantage from dynamics and impressive performance on large-scale read-world image datasets.

 We sincerely ask you and other fellow reviewers to consider our efforts and what we have achieved on this work again.


[a] Li, Yuhang, et al. Differentiable spike: Rethinking gradient-descent for training spiking neural networks. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 23426-23439.


Authors of paper 1225

content.title: Concerns addressed, but writing should be clearer.
content.comment:
Dear authors, 

Thank you for clarifying computational complexity, neuromorphic hardware, and bio-inspired comparison methods. You addressed my main concerns; a comparison to other bio-inspired methods and proper situating in the related works would be nice for a revision.

I acknowledge that the writing has improved substantially, but I concur with reviewer r6pt that the paper is still too hard to parse to transmit your message.  

Moreover, I still would recommend a grammar checker. Sorry for being so repetitive, but this may be the easiest (and free) way to improve your writing. Here, for example, how your abstract looks after:

This paper investigates the dynamics-inspired neuromorphic architecture for neural representation and learning following Hamilton's principle. The proposed approach converts weight-based neural structure to its dynamics-based form that consists of finite sub-models, whose mutual relations measured by computing path integrals amongst their dynamic states are equivalent to the typical neural weights. Based on the entropy reduction process derived from the Euler- Lagrange equations, the feedback signals interpreted as stress forces amongst sub-models push them to move. We first train a dynamics-based neural model from scratch and observe that this model outperforms its corresponding feedforward neural networks on the MNIST dataset. Then we convert several pre-trained neural structures (e.g., DenseNet, ResNet, Transformers) into dynamics-based forms, followed by fine-tuning via entropy reduction to obtain the stabilized dynamic states. We observe consistent improvements of these transformed models on the ImageNet dataset regarding computational complexity, the number of trainable units, testing accuracy, and robustness. Moreover, we demonstrate the correlation between the performance of a neural system and its structural entropy. 

An article was missing, and a sentence was poorly structured. One phrase was wordy and using "etc." in formal writing is frowned upon.

Other minor points:
- Dyn instead of DyN in conclusion
- Punctuation of equations, maybe you find this useful: Mermin, N. D. (1989). "What's wrong with these equations? ". Physics Today, 42(10), 9. https://wiki.physics.udel.edu/wiki_phys600/images/3/39/MERMIN%3Dwhats_wrong_with_these_equations.pdf

I updated my score. For acceptance, I think a significant rewrite is necessary. Please don't be disheartened. Your work seems compelling but hard to comprehend in its current form. With more precise writing, the impact and reach of your work will be considerably higher, ultimately more important than mere publication.

Best wishes and success for future submissions!

content.comment:
Q6: How does relate to the neurological fact afterwards? (third paragraph). 

A6: Our method is biologically inspired by Hebb's learning rule, as discussed in the revised paper. The biological validation is also related to several biological experiments. For example, the most recent biological research from Stanford [f] shows that human brain tissue implanted in rats as stem cells prompt excitement like the human brain after 143 days or more. Thus, it is reasonable to conclude that the brain neurons have sufficient information to guide how the neural connections between them are generated. We have revised the paper for more clarity.


Q7: In which regard exactly is the implementation more efficient?

A7: As we have discussed and compared in the paper, the efficiency comes from the significantly reduced parameters, since in DyN we only need to record the neuron states rather than their weights. Moreover, the most important calculation in the DyN system is the path integral among neuron states, which can be realized in a computation-free manner by other types of hardware systems such as liquid-crystal structure[g]. Therefore, we provide the corresponding computation complexity statistics regarding to this in both Table 1 and 2. Despite that the hardware issue is beyond the scope of this paper, we believe that this can be used a guidance for the development of hardware for neuromorphic learning models in the future.


Q8: Why would one need to use a noisy physical system for computation?

A8: Our model involves the computation of path integral between neuronal states rather than weight-based update, which can hardly be implemented efficiently with current hardware architecture, as discussed in the response of the last question. However, it may be easier and more accurate if we use hardware of other forms, e.g., the liquid crystal devices or optical computing devises. In the current implementation, due to the quantization error in digitalization, the model parameters, i.e., the neuronal state, can only be maintained at a specific resolution. From the mechanism aspect, our architecture merges the weight parameters that are originally independent of each other into a compact but more interacted neural states. So the sensitivity of the model parameters to noise must be considered. We have revised the paper in the introduction part (paragraph 4) for more discussion.


Q9: training times and variance?

A9: In our revised paper, we repeat MNIST experiments without halving resolution in a deeper NN and present a new table with more convincing results, as shown in Table 1. The training procedure for each configuration is repeated 20 times to calculate its variance, and the results are stable and statistically significant. By replacing the fully connected layer in a typical ANN with our DyN subsystems, the top1-TestAcc has improved from 97.955+/-0.032 to 98.215+/-0.013 with 7.9% parameters retained. We also report results on LeNet and it DyN variant.

Q10: No.TUs vs No.Params

A10: Actually, No.TUs is equivalent to No.Params, since the dynamic states of each sub-model can be efficiently encoded as a single trainable parameter via a Cantor’s space. We mistakenly used the term “units” because we would like to emphasize the “parameters” that act as a dynamical unit rather than a Float Tensor. In the revision, we have removed the No. TUs to better clarify this issue.


Q11: performance without adjustment?

A11: In the revised version, we present Table 2 that present the Top1-acc on ImageNet to compare the “ideal” models that have not been affected by “noise”. It can be shown that the performance is not sensitive to the noise, which can also provide possibility in further acceleration via techniques such as hashing towards a more efficient neuromorphic computing architecture.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Here the authors describe a framework for utilizing what they deem "dynamics-based models", which they contrast with the standard static models used in deep learning. The framework describes a method for training dynamics-based models to approximate non-linear functions. As a proof of principle, their method is used to achieve reasonable performance on MNIST. Secondly, and perhaps more impressively, they derive a method to transform a typical weight-based ANN to a dynamics-based model. They find that the dynamics-based equivalent to a standard ANN is much more computationally efficient while retaining good classification performance on ImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**


1. As far as I know, the method they propose is novel, and many of the ideas presented in the manuscript are genuinely interesting.
2. The results presented for ImageNet appear to be very impressive.

**Weaknesses**

1. The paper is very hard to follow, especially for a machine learning audience.
	1. I am using this as an example, but this paragraph is attempting to communicate a central claim of the manuscript. On p. 2 “…weights are mathematically trivial.” I am still confused about what is meant by this paragraph. This sentence is then followed by “This claim is biologically well supported…” Why is the triviality of neural network weights *biologically and mathematically supported?* A critical point is being made here, but because the language is unnecessarily abstract I cannot determine what it is or why it is reasonable, either from a biological or mathematical point of view.
	2. As another example, in the caption for Figure 1, “Weights are mathematically equivalent to the path integral between dynamic states of sub-models (highly functional neurons)”. Concretely, what is meant by dynamical state and sub-model? What is a highly functional neuron? 
	3. The included diagrams are under-labeled, e.g. Figure 1b and Figure 5.
2. The MNIST benchmark can be solved by “standard” weight-based models with many fewer trainable parameters. For instance, a quick scouring of Kaggle and Github will turn up convolutional models with on the order of 5-10k trainable parameters with nearly 98-99% accuracy on MNIST. 
	1. On a related note, what are the training and inference runtimes of DyN vs. the 2-layer network presented in Figure 1? I am not comfortable enough with the author’s formalism to know if REMs and MACs should be considered equivalent metrics of computational complexity.

content.title: Point-to-Point Response to Reviewer r6pt
content.comment:
Thanks for the constructive comments and suggestions! The responses to the questions are listed below.


Q1: Why is the triviality of neural weights biologically and mathematically supported?

A1: The triviality of neural weights can be mathematically validated based on our proposed principle of dynamic subsystems, which is an alternative to Cybenko’s Universal approximation theorem, except that our trainable units are the neuronal dynamics rather than the neural weights. Our method is biologically inspired by Hebb's learning rule, as discussed in the revised paper. The biological validation is also related to several biological experiments. For example, the most recent biological research from Stanford [a] shows that human brain tissue implanted in rats as stem cells prompt excitement like the human brain after 143 days or more. Thus, it is reasonable to conclude that the brain neurons have sufficient information to guide how the neural connections between them are generated. We have revised the paper for more clarity.


Q2: What are sub-model and dynamical states?

A2: In the revised manuscript, we further elaborate on the definitions of many fundamental concepts used in the paper. For instance, a neuron's dynamic states (aka. neuronal dynamics), e.g., spatial location, velocity, acceleration, activation/inhibition state, etc., can be described in a specific phase space in which neurons that are located close to each other or have similar dynamic patterns are closer together.
To distinguish them from node-like neurons in the computational sense, we use the concept of sub-models. A sub-model is a highly functional neuron capable of receiving or emitting signals and changing its dynamic states. Moreover, a group of sub-models sharing identical global settings (e.g., a specified hidden layer in an ANN) is collectively referred to as a subsystem.


Q3: Comparison on more SoTA approaches on MNIST benchmark?

A3: The purpose of the MNIST experiment was designed to examine the subsystem's performance, i.e., how much the performance would be improved if the neural weights of a given fully connected or convolutional layer were replaced by the neuronal dynamics. Therefore, we only did comparison experiments for some smaller and more representative models rather than SoTA-models. To better address the reviewer concern, in the revision of the manuscript, we perform substitution-comparison experiments (replacing the fully connected and convolutional layers with DyN subsystems) for the deeper MLP model and the convolutional model like LeNet-5 and repeated each set of experiments 20 times to calculate its variance. The results show that the replaced model can achieve a stable accuracy rate improvement of about 0.18%, and the parameter size and computational complexity can be significantly reduced. Due to the time limit, we would like to provide more results by converting more traditional SoTA models into Dyn counterparts in the following days.


Q4: What are the training and inference time of DyN vs. the 2-layer network presented in Figure 1?

A4: The training time of DyN may fluctuate, depending on the initialization and pre-set thresholds. For example, during the training process of LeNet-5, a single iteration takes about 22-25 seconds, while DyN takes between 12-145 seconds. The inference time of a LeNet and its DyN is basically the same. We will include more analysis on the training/testing time in the revision, once we finish the comprehensive experimental validation.


Q5: If REMs and MACs should be considered equivalent metrics of computational complexity?

A5: For more clarity, in the Table 1 and Table 2 of the revised manuscript, we evaluate the computational complexity of a DyN model in two ways. The first way is following the traditional metric of computational complexity, i.e., the number of floating-point operations (FLOPs). The second way, recorded in the brackets next to the traditional one, is treating the path integral operation as zero-complexity operation, which can be achieved by some material such as the liquid crystal structures [b]. Accordingly, we have revised the corresponding part in the revision.

[a] J Gray Camp and Barbara Treutlein. Human brain organoids influence rat behaviour, 2022

[b] Rui Zhang, Steven A Redford, Paul V Ruijgrok, Nitin Kumar, Ali Mozaffari, Sasha Zemsky,
Aaron R Dinner, Vincenzo Vitelli, Zev Bryant, Margaret L Gardel, et al. Spatiotemporal con-
trol of liquid crystal structure and dynamics through activity patterning. Nature materials, 20(6): 875–882, 2021.

First I want to thank the authors for their detailed response, which addresses some of my concerns but not all. Q2-Q5 are adequately taken care of, and so I have revised my score accordingly.

However, my main overarching concern is that this paper is still very difficult to follow. Echoing the other reviewer, the manuscript still has a number of grammatical errors. Secondly, more importantly I don't think I understand what the authors are trying to communicate. Why is a neural weight *trivial*? I still don't follow what the authors are trying to say here. Are you saying that they are trivial because they can be replaced with your dynamics-based framework? If so then the word trivial is inappropriate here and unnecessarily inflammatory. Additionally, what precisely is the argument from the stem cell implantation study and why it supports the biological plausibility of the author's argument? I still don't quite follow the argument that connected cells should have similar dynamics. 

I encourage the authors to resubmit this work, because it does appear genuinely innovative; however, the writing is a big obstacle.

content.title: Thanks for your suggestion
content.comment:
Thanks for your inspirational and kind suggestions. As you suggested, we modify the term "trivial" as "covariates," which is more precise to our purpose: to explore the nature of neural weights. 

From biological aspect, the brain cell implantation study in the referred paper shows that the brain cells can generate and evolve the neural weights connecting them. This provides some indirect evidence support on our study. However, we decide to remove this part of discussion in order to avoid the misunderstanding from a broad range of readers. 

Accordingly, the revised discussion in the Introduction is presented below:

" Furthermore, we prove that the neural weights are covariates of neuronal dynamics, as shown in Eq. 1 and Appendix. A. This finding provides an alternative insight on the interaction between neurons from the dynamics perspective, and informative guidance on how to conduct efficient learning in an neuromorphic manner. "

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a dynamics-inspired neuromorphic architecture, DyN, for neural representation, trying to find an efficient neural mechanism compatible with evolving neural topologies. To achieve the goal, they replace the typical neural weights with the path integrals between neuronal dynamics, which are explicitly interpreted as the Euclidean distances between sub-models in the experiments. The relevant update rules are derived from a dynamics-inspired view and seem consistent with the back-propagation algorithm. They first train a dynamics-inspired neuromorphic model from scratch to compete with its counterpart, a 2-layer MLP, on MNIST to conclude that their dynamics-based neural representation learning outperforms the traditional weight-based one. Then they transform several mainstream pre-trained neural models using the DyN mechanism and validate them on popular benchmark ImageNet. Experiments demonstrate the good performance and the relationship between a model’s structural entropy and performance. This result implicitly validates their claim that structural learning with neuronal dynamics is significant.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. Novelty: the paper is possibly the first to cancel out the neural weights that are significant to the DL community. Though some weight-agnostic approaches have been presented, they have not been convinced that neural weights are just hidden states of some more essential variables, e.g., neuronal dynamics.

2. Inspiration: the paper presents an efficient neuromorphic architecture. This work would inspire the algorithmic study and the development of neuromorphic computing technologies that require consistency with dynamics-based approaches.

3. Experimental evaluation: the proposed models outperform their counterparts on widely used datasets in terms of testing accuracy, computational complexity, and robustness to parameter noises during the inference stage. The authors also present an exciting correlation between the model’s structural entropy and performance.

Weakness:
1) Some writing issues: 

    a) The paper’s claim (neural weights are mathematically trivial) appears to be related to Theorem A.1, but this relationship has not been explicitly claimed in the main paper. 

    b)The significance of Hamilton’s principle and the Euler-Lagrange equation for the learning stage should be further elaborated. 

    c)The principle of hierarchical structures in section 3.2 seems irrelevant to the main claim that neural weights are trivial; the authors need to include a detailed interpretation of this proposed principle and its significance to the overall system. 

    d)Though the consistency of this dynamics-inspired method with the back-propagation algorithm is evident and undoubtful, the relevant proof in Appendix B still requires further elaboration. 

    e)The relation between Theorem A.1 in Appendix A and the universal approximation theorem should be claimed with more clarification.
2) Some experimental issues: 

    a)The paper should provide testing results on the performance of cases with an ideal resolution.
 
    b)The authors might need more design on experiments that show how the hyper-parameters (e.g., number of subsystems, dimension of sub-models, learning rate for DyN) affect model performance. 

    c)An ablation study should be included if the page limit allows it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Clarity and quality: the paper’s clarity and readability need further improvement; some interrelated arguments and discussions are scattered throughout the article, and some essential propositions are not included in the main paper but the appendices. 

2. Novelty: it is an excellent work, which is likely the first to interpret the traditional neural weights as the relations amongst neuronal dynamics using dynamics-inspired methods. 

3. Reproducibility: acceptable overall, but the computational efficiency requires further validation in the actual implementation case.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper could contribute heavily to the neural representation community since it offers an inspirational alternative that is efficient and highly consistent with the future trend of neuromorphic computing. One of the most significant contributions of this paper is that it reveals the possibility that an artificial neural network can be accessible to a dynamics-oriented mechanism, which might bring deep learning to a truly physical implementation. The paper has the merit of establishing a bridge between artificial and biological neural networks; thus, it would inspire further works that contribute heavily to the ML community. A few parts need some clarification on theoretical demonstrations and experiments. I would like to see clarifications and modifications from the authors.

content.title: Point-to-Point Response to Reviewer KJEX
content.comment:
Thanks for the constructive comments and suggestions! The responses to the questions are listed below.

Q1: Relation with Universal Approximation Theorem?

A1: The typical UATs demonstrate the approximation capacities of neural networks by training the neural weights. At the same time, the principle of dynamic subsystems (presented in the appendix and has now been placed in the preliminary) provides an alternative to the typical UATs. This result shows that the approximation capacities of neural structures can be obtained by training the neurons rather than the neural weights connecting the neurons. To make things clearer, we have revised the paper accordingly. We hopefully that the revision can address your concern.


Q2: Significance of Hamilton’s Principle and the Euler-Lagrange’s equation?

A2: These results, inspired by physics, guarantee the efficiency of applying path integral in building a more complicated structure. Besides, these results lead to a computation-friendly version of the proposed update rules that show equivalence to entropy reduction. Therefore, a physical formulation can obtain the proposed learning and inference mechanisms. We have revised the paper for more clarity.


Q3: Performance without adjustment?

A3: In the revised version, we present Table 2 that present the Top1-acc on ImageNet to compare the “ideal” models that have not been affected by “noise”. It can be shown that the performance is not sensitive to the noise, which can also provide possibility in further acceleration via techniques such as hashing towards a more efficient neuromorphic computing architecture.


Q4: Hyper-parameters.

A4: Detailed experiments regarding hyper-parameters and feature ablations are presented in the appendix, and more details will be posted in the open-source coding platform (e.g., Github).

content.title: Some more results on MNIST
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and AC, 

Regarding to the performance on MNIST, we further validate our method applied in LeNet-5 with different hyperparameters, i.e., the number of subsystems. Each set of evaluations is repeated 10 times to eliminate the noise. The experimental results are presented below:

|   Model Type  | No.Subsys  | No.Params | TestAcc (%) |
|:------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------:|:----------------:|
|     LeNet5      |                     |      61.80k    |      99.04     |
| LeNet5+DyN | 3+3+2+2+2 |       2.03k     |      98.75      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 4+4+3+3+3 |      2.76k      |      99.05      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 5+5+5+5+5 |      4.09k      |      99.16      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 8+8+5+5+5 |      4.42k      |      99.20      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 8+8+6+6+6 |      5.04k      |      99.21      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 7+7+7+7+7 |      5.54k      |      99.24      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 5+5+8+8+8 |      5.94k      |      99.23      |
| LeNet5+DyN | 8+8+8+8+8 |      6.27k      |      99.22      |


As shown in the table, by converting the convolutional layers and fully connected layers of LeNet-5 into DyN blocks, the model’s performance improves (99.04% --> 99.24%) with fewer parameters (61.8k --> 5.54k). Additionally, instead of building F*F subsystems for a convolutional filter of shape F*F, we found that using an F+F subsystems such that the (i,j) element of the filter is the dynamical relation between subsystems Pi and Pj, then we notice that the performance still improves. This idea is similar as the decomposition of 7*7 convolution into 1*7 and 7*1  convolutions in Inception-v3 [a].

[a] Szegedy, Christian, et al. "Rethinking the inception architecture for computer vision." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2016.
